**Part 1 – Personal biography**  

I’m a 50‑year‑old logistics manager living in Zaltbommel, a town that stretches along the Waal River. After completing a vocational diploma in transport engineering at the ROC in ’92, I earned a bachelor’s degree in Business Administration from Utrecht University, which helped me move from the warehouse floor to the coordination office.  

My wife Marieke runs a small boutique bakery on the market square, and together we raise our two kids—Emma, 16, who plays the cello in the school orchestra, and Lars, 14, a forward on the local soccer team. Our mornings start with a 20‑kilometre bike ride along the riverbank; I drop the kids at school, then head to the distribution centre where I oversee the daily routing of fresh produce to supermarkets across the province.  

When I’m not at work, I spend evenings in the garage building wooden furniture—most recently a reclaimed‑oak dining table for our friends’ anniversary. On weekends I help coach the junior soccer squad, tend the garden, and visit the weekly farmers’ market where I pick up seasonal vegetables and chat with the growers. I value punctuality, hands‑on problem solving, and the sense of community that comes from knowing my neighbours’ names.  

**Part 2 – Political outlook**  

My daily work hinges on reliable roads, bridges, and digital systems that keep freight moving smoothly. When a new weight‑limit regulation threatened to bottleneck our routes, I saw firsthand how excessive red tape can hurt small‑to‑medium enterprises and raise costs for families like mine. That experience made me prioritize pragmatic governance—policies that streamline procedures without compromising safety.  

Raising two children in a town where schools depend on steady funding has reinforced my belief that education must be well‑resourced, yet I’m wary of budget overruns that force higher taxes. Watching Marieke’s bakery navigate rising energy prices reminded me how essential affordable utilities are for local businesses.  

Because the VVD’s platform emphasizes fiscal responsibility, sensible investment in infrastructure, and a balanced approach to public spending, I felt it best reflected the practical outcomes I need for work, family, and community. That’s why I cast my vote for the VVD in the last election.

**Part 1 – Personal biography**  

I’m a 25‑year‑old man living in Almere, a city that still feels a bit like a construction site but is growing fast enough to keep me busy. After finishing a mixed track of Havo, VWO and an MBO‑4 program in logistics, I landed a junior coordinator role at a regional distribution centre just outside the town. My workday usually starts at 7 a.m.; I ride my commuter bike along the new bike lanes, grab a coffee at the corner bakery, and spend the morning tracking incoming shipments and updating the warehouse management system.  

I share a modest two‑bedroom apartment with a fellow student‑turned‑designer. On weekends we host a small house‑concert where I play bass in a garage‑band that covers everything from Dutch folk to indie rock. I also tend a plot in the community garden on the fourth floor of our building; it’s my excuse to get my hands dirty and meet neighbours over tomatoes and herbs.  

When I’m not cycling or rehearsing, I’m scrolling through tech podcasts, experimenting with home‑cooking (my specialty is poffertjes with a twist of orange zest), and planning short trips to the nearby Oostvaardersplassen for a bit of bird‑watching. I value reliability, a bit of humor, and the feeling of a job well done, whether it’s a perfectly timed delivery or a garden plot that finally yields its first carrots.  

---

**Part 2 – Political biography**  

I didn’t cast a ballot in the 2030 election, but I did vote for D66 in the 2021 national vote. My daily commute on the bike lanes that the party championed made me appreciate their focus on sustainable transport; without those lanes, my ride would be a hazard rather than a pleasure. Working in logistics, I see first‑hand how supply‑chain bottlenecks affect small businesses, so I support policies that streamline regulations while still protecting workers’ rights.  

Living in Almere’s rapidly expanding housing market, I’ve felt the pressure of rising rents and the scarcity of affordable family‑size homes. That experience drives my interest in pragmatic urban‑planning measures that balance growth with livability. My involvement in the community garden has also made me attentive to local environmental initiatives—things like subsidies for rooftop solar and support for urban green spaces feel tangible and worthwhile.  

Overall, my political stance is shaped by the concrete ways policies intersect with my commute, my job, and my neighbourhood. I look for parties that translate broad ideas into everyday improvements, rather than grand rhetoric that never reaches the bike lane outside my door.

**Part 1 – Personal biography**

I grew up in a modest neighbourhood on the west side of Leeuwarden, where the scent of fresh‑baked bread from the local bakery still drifts through the streets each morning. After finishing my secondary schooling, I completed a one‑year technical program that led me to an apprenticeship as a cabinet‑maker. For the past four decades I have run a small workshop on the Oudegracht, crafting wooden furniture for families across the province.  

My wife, Marijke, and I raised two children in the same house where I now live with our golden retriever, Bink. Weekends are usually spent tending to the garden behind the house, where I grow tomatoes, herbs, and a few rows of tulips that I sell at the Saturday market. I’m an avid cyclist and make a point of riding the flat, wind‑blown routes along the canals whenever the weather allows.  

Music is a constant companion; I still play the accordion at the local senior club’s folk evenings. I also volunteer once a month at the community centre, helping newcomers learn basic Dutch and sharing stories about the city’s maritime history. My evenings often end with a cup of black tea while I read the regional newspaper and keep up with the latest developments in sustainable building practices.

**Part 2 – Political perspective**

Having spent a lifetime building and maintaining homes, I’ve seen how housing costs and energy prices affect families at every stage. My own pension is modest, and the rising cost of heating makes winter evenings feel colder than they should. That’s why I value policies that protect pension income and promote affordable, energy‑efficient retrofits for older homes.  

Healthcare is another daily concern; I’ve watched my parents navigate a system that sometimes feels stretched thin, and I rely on regular visits to the local clinic for my own check‑ups. Ensuring that senior care remains accessible and that waiting times stay short feels essential to a dignified later life.  

I also care about public transport that connects the outskirts of Leeuwarden to the city centre without forcing us to drive, especially as my eyesight isn’t what it used to be. Reliable buses and well‑maintained cycle paths let me stay active and independent.  

These practical experiences guided my decision to vote for **50PLUS** in the 2030 election, because the party’s focus on pension security, healthcare accessibility, and age‑friendly infrastructure aligns with the everyday realities I and many of my peers face.

**Part 1 – Personal biography**

I’m 34 and have lived my whole life in the quiet stretch of Horst aan de Maas, where the river Maas curls around the town like a familiar ribbon. After finishing my bachelor’s in environmental science at the University of Utrecht, I returned home and took a position as a project coordinator for the regional water‑management office. My days start early: I bike the six kilometres to the office, stopping at the bakery on the corner for a croissant and a strong coffee. 

At home I share a modest, renovated farmhouse with my partner, Jeroen, and our three‑year‑old daughter, Lotte. We keep a small vegetable patch in the back garden, where Lotte loves to pull carrots while I experiment with heirloom tomatoes. On weekends we often drive the family car to the weekly market in Venlo, where I pick up fresh herbs and chat with the stallholders about the upcoming flood‑risk workshops I’m organizing. 

In my spare time I’m an avid reader of Dutch historical fiction, a volunteer guide at the local museum, and a member of a cycling club that meets every Thursday for a 30‑kilometre ride through the Limburg countryside. I enjoy cooking meals that blend the regional flavors I grew up with and the new techniques I pick up from cooking classes in Maastricht.

**Part 2 – Political perspective**

My work dealing with water levels and flood prevention has made me acutely aware of how climate change can turn a familiar river into a threat. Seeing the direct impact on our farms and the extra strain on local infrastructure pushes me to support policies that invest in resilient water‑management systems and renewable energy. Because I rely on a reliable public transport network to commute by bike and occasional train, I favour improvements to regional transit that make it easier for people in smaller towns to connect without a car.  

Having a young child, I’m also concerned about the quality of early‑education facilities; my experience coordinating community workshops showed me how much a well‑resourced school can lift a neighbourhood. I therefore look for parties that prioritize education funding and give teachers the tools they need.  

Balancing a modest household budget with the desire to keep our garden thriving, I appreciate fiscal responsibility that doesn’t sacrifice long‑term environmental projects. All these factors led me to cast my vote for D66 in the 2030 election, because their platform aligns with the practical steps I see as necessary for our town’s future.

**Part 1 – Personal Biography**

I’m 33 and have lived in the same Dutch city my whole life. After finishing Havo and VWO, I completed a two‑year MBO program in graphic design, which led to a junior position at a local advertising agency. Over the years I’ve moved from a shared flat to a modest townhouse I now share with my partner, Maya, and our 7‑year‑old Labrador, Luna. Mornings usually start with a 30‑minute bike ride along the river, a habit I picked up during university to avoid the rush‑hour traffic. I’m an avid home‑cook; on weekends I experiment with seasonal Dutch produce, often inviting friends over for a simple dinner and a game of board‑games. When I’m not designing, I volunteer once a month at the community centre, helping teenagers learn basic digital skills. I’m a regular at the local library, where I’m currently reading a biography of a pioneering Dutch botanist. Music is a big part of my life—I play a bit of acoustic guitar and enjoy attending intimate live‑music venues. I try to keep a balance between work, creativity, and the small rituals that make everyday life feel grounded.

**Part 2 – Political Perspective**

My daily commute on well‑maintained bike lanes and my reliance on reliable public transport have shown me how much a city’s infrastructure can shape quality of life. When I see the city invest in expanding cycling routes or upgrading digital connectivity for small businesses, I feel the tangible benefits of forward‑thinking policies. Watching the younger generation at the community centre struggle with outdated software sparked my belief that education must keep pace with technological change. Climate‑related flooding in low‑lying neighborhoods reminded me that long‑term environmental planning isn’t optional—it directly affects the safety of families like mine. These experiences have guided my vote for D66, a party that consistently pushes for progressive education reforms, robust climate action, and investment in digital infrastructure. I support candidates who prioritize pragmatic solutions over rhetoric, because I’ve seen how sensible policy can improve everyday routines and future opportunities.

After a quick shower, I brew a strong cup of coffee and pack the kids’ lunches—Mila, 6, and Finn, 4—before we all head out. We cycle the three kilometres to the primary school where I teach Dutch and social studies; the route takes me past the edge of the Veluwe, where the pine scent always reminds me why I love nature.

On weekends I tend the community‑garden plot I share with neighbours; we grow kale, tomatoes and a few herbs, swapping tips and produce. I’m an avid reader of contemporary Dutch fiction and I run a small book club that meets monthly at the local library. I value reliability, curiosity, and the feeling that small actions can add up to something larger.

My vote for GL‑PvdA comes from everyday realities I see in my classroom and neighbourhood. The same concern extends to families I meet after school; many worry about rising rents that push them farther from jobs and schools. Caring for an aging parent has shown me how fragile our health‑care system can be, especially when appointments are hard to secure. I appreciate GL‑PvdA’s focus on expanding home‑care services and keeping medication affordable. **Part 1 – Personal profile**  

I’m a 53‑year‑old who has lived my whole life in the flat, green‑spotted landscape of Westland. After finishing my Vmbo and a short stint in the havo‑vwo track, I earned an MBO‑1 certificate in agricultural technology, which led me straight into the greenhouse sector that dominates our municipality. For the past three decades I’ve worked as a maintenance coordinator for a family‑run tomato operation, making sure the climate‑control systems stay humming and the irrigation lines stay clear.  

My husband and I raised two children here; both have moved out—one is a primary‑school teacher in Delft, the other runs a bike‑repair shop in The Hague. On weekends I still help out at the local community garden, swapping seed packets and tips with neighbours. I love cycling the narrow dikes early in the morning, stopping at the market to buy fresh herbs and a stroopwafel. In my spare time I read historical novels and keep a modest scrapbook of the changing greenhouse roofs that line our streets. Family gatherings, quiet evenings with a cup of tea, and the rhythm of the greenhouse season are what keep me grounded.  

**Part 2 – Political outlook**  

Working day in and day out with the practicalities of greenhouse heating, water use, and labor schedules has taught me how tightly our livelihoods depend on reliable infrastructure and fair regulations. When I see a new policy that could raise energy costs for growers without offering a clear transition plan, I worry about the ripple effect on small operators like the one my husband and I helped start. Conversely, I appreciate measures that protect the soil and water quality, because I’ve watched a neighbor’s fields suffer when runoff isn’t managed properly.  

My voting choices reflect a desire for pragmatic stewardship of the countryside: I voted for the BoerBurgerBeweging (BBB) because they focus on giving growers a voice in national decisions, support sensible subsidies for sustainable tech, and push for regional input on zoning. I’m not drawn to grand rhetoric; I look for concrete proposals that keep our farms viable, maintain the local job market, and preserve the landscape that shaped my life.

**Part 1 – Personal biography**

I wake up before sunrise most days to the sound of my border collie, Luna, nudging my ankle. After a quick jog along the dikes that ring our village, I bike the ten kilometres to the regional health office where I coordinate outreach programs for seniors and new parents. My mornings are a mix of planning community workshops, field‑visiting care homes, and answering calls from neighbours who need help navigating the healthcare system.

When I’m not at work, I’m in the kitchen experimenting with recipes that blend traditional Dutch staples with the spices I picked up on a trip to Suriname last summer. On Saturdays I head to the farmers’ market, where I sell jars of homemade pickles and pick up fresh herbs for my herb garden behind the house. In the evenings I often unwind with a novel by Maarten ’t Hart or a documentary about renewable energy, and I make a point of reading the local newspaper to stay informed about municipal decisions.

Family is a cornerstone of my life: my partner, a carpenter, and I share a modest, solar‑powered home where we host occasional dinner gatherings for friends and neighbours. I’m an avid cyclist, a volunteer docent at the village library, and I try to embed a sense of stewardship for our landscape in everything I do.  

**Part 2 – Political biography**

Living in a spread‑out community where the nearest train station is a fifteen‑minute drive has made reliable public transport and good broadband feel essential, not optional. My work exposing me to the gaps in home‑care services for the elderly convinced me that a flexible, well‑funded health system is a matter of dignity. Watching the impact of climate‑related flooding on nearby fields reinforced my belief that proactive water management and renewable‑energy incentives can protect both livelihoods and the environment.

Because I see education as the engine that lets people adapt to change, I support policies that keep schools well‑resourced and promote lifelong learning opportunities. The party I chose in the last election, D66, aligns with my desire for pragmatic solutions: stronger digital infrastructure for rural areas, clear climate targets that respect our agricultural heritage, and a health system that balances efficiency with personal care. My vote reflects the everyday realities I encounter—whether it’s ensuring Luna can safely cross a bike lane or that my neighbours can access tele‑health appointments without a long commute.

**Part 1 – Personal biography**

I’m a 19‑year‑old from the village of Mook in the Land van Cuijk municipality. After finishing primary school, I’ve been working part‑time at the bakery on the main street, where I open the ovens at six a.m. and hand out fresh croissants to regulars before school lets out. My parents still live in the house we grew up in; I share a small bedroom with my younger sister, who is in her final year of secondary school.  

Every weekday I bike to work, then walk home to help my mother with the garden—especially the tomato beds she’s been tending since the pandemic. On weekends I meet a group of friends for a quick football match on the local field, and we usually finish with a walk along the Maas, where I like to try my hand at fishing. I’m a regular at the community centre, where I volunteer once a month to sort donations for the local food bank. Reliability and looking after the people around me are the values I try to live by.

**Part 2 – Political biography**

Living in a tight‑knit rural community has taught me how much everyday services matter. When the bus schedule was cut back last year, I saw my friends struggle to get to work or to the nearest train station, and it made me think about the importance of accessible public transport for young people like me. The bakery where I work depends on a steady flow of local customers; any downturn in the regional economy hits us hard, so I’m especially attentive to policies that support small businesses and vocational training.

I’ve also noticed how the river’s water quality has worsened, affecting both my hobby of fishing and the health of the local ecosystem. That experience pushes me to prioritize environmental stewardship, but I’m wary of proposals that would raise taxes without clear benefits for our community.

In the 2030 election I chose not to cast a ballot because none of the platforms addressed the concrete issues I face daily—public transport, support for small enterprises, and realistic environmental measures. If I had voted, I would have leaned toward a party that balances social investment with pragmatic economic policies, one that understands the everyday realities of villages like mine.

**Part 1 – Personal Biography**

I was born and raised in a modest neighbourhood on the outskirts of ’s‑Hertogenbosch, where the streets still echo with the sounds of the weekly market. After finishing my secondary education at the local Havo, I completed a two‑year vocational programme in textile technology and spent the next three decades working as a pattern‑maker for a family‑run textile mill that supplied fabrics to regional designers. When the mill closed in the early 2000s, I transitioned to part‑time teaching at the nearby mbo, sharing practical skills with apprentices.

My husband, a retired civil‑engineer, and I have lived in the same terraced house for over forty years. Our daughter moved to Amsterdam for university and now visits us a few times a year with her two children. I’m an avid gardener; my rose beds and vegetable patch are the pride of the street, and I spend Saturday mornings at the local library reading historical novels and gardening magazines. I volunteer once a month at the community centre, helping organise the senior‑citizen bingo evenings, and I never miss the annual city lantern festival, where I meet old school friends over coffee and stroopwafels.

**Part 2 – Political Biography**

Having spent most of my adult life in a small‑scale, family‑oriented business, I value stability and the sense that local institutions can be trusted to look after their members. When the textile mill shut down, the support I received from the municipality—grants for retraining and the preservation of our historic factory building—showed me how practical policies can make a real difference. That experience has shaped my belief that government should play a constructive role in safeguarding traditional industries while encouraging modest innovation.

I also see the importance of maintaining affordable housing for seniors like myself, especially as property prices rise in the city centre. The policies I’ve observed that protect home ownership and provide tax relief for long‑term residents have directly helped me keep my home without financial strain. Because I rely on reliable public services—healthcare, transport, and community facilities—I tend to support parties that prioritize responsible budgeting and incremental improvements over sweeping reforms.

These considerations lead me to vote for the Christian Democratic Appeal (CDA). I feel the party’s pragmatic approach aligns with my desire for steady stewardship of the community, support for small businesses, and policies that respect both tradition and the modest needs of everyday citizens.

I’m a 19‑year‑old living on the island of Goeree‑Overflakkee. After finishing the lower tracks of secondary school, I’m now in my second year of an MBO 1 program that trains me in horticultural techniques. Most weekdays I split my time between classes, a part‑time shift at the local fish‑market where I help sort the daily catch, and evenings spent in the community garden that my neighbours run on a vacant lot near the dike.  

My family runs a small dairy farm a few kilometres from the market, so I grew up helping with milking and feeding the cows, which gave me a practical sense of where food comes from. On weekends I love cycling the flat, wind‑blown paths that connect the villages, and I’m an avid reader of contemporary Dutch crime novels – the kind that let me picture the very streets I ride through.  

I’m curious by nature, so I volunteer once a month to teach younger kids how to plant seedlings, hoping they’ll appreciate the land as much as I do. In my spare time I experiment with preserving the fish I sell, turning it into spreads and pickles that I share with friends.  

**PART 2 – Political biography (150 words)**  

My everyday encounters with the island’s fragile ecosystems have made climate resilience a personal priority. Watching the salt‑marsh edges shrink after a storm convinced me that local agriculture needs stronger support for sustainable practices, and that public transport must be reliable enough for young people who don’t own a car.  

When I finally went to the polling station, I chose GroenLinks because their proposals for renewable energy subsidies and investment in regional education felt grounded in the realities I see: more funding for vocational training, better cycling infrastructure, and policies that protect our wetlands.  

I’ve also been frustrated by the limited job prospects for teenagers after school; the party’s focus on apprenticeships and youth entrepreneurship resonated with my own experience of juggling work and study. While I didn’t cast a vote in the last election, the combination of personal observations and the desire for a greener, more inclusive local economy motivated me to support a platform that aligns with the practical changes I hope to see on the island.

**Part 1 – Personal Biography**

I’m 65 and have spent most of my adult life in the quiet villages that dot De Fryslân Marren. After completing an Hbo program in agricultural engineering, I earned a bachelor’s degree in environmental management at the University of Groningen. For thirty‑seven years I worked as a water‑management specialist for the provincial authority, overseeing the maintenance of dikes and drainage canals that keep our low‑lying fields arable. I retired two years ago, but I still volunteer on the local water board’s advisory committee.

My wife, Marijke, and I have lived in the same farmhouse on the edge of the lake for nearly four decades. Our two children live in Leeuwarden and Utrecht, and we enjoy the weekly visits of our three grandchildren, who love feeding the ducks at the pond. My mornings begin with a walk along the dike, a cup of black coffee, and the day’s edition of *Friesch Dagblad*. In my spare time I tend to a small vegetable garden, restore old wooden boats, and attend the weekly choir at our Reformed church.

**Part 2 – Political Biography**

The way my life has unfolded in this water‑rich, close‑knit community shapes how I look at politics. Having spent a career ensuring that the canals work, I value reliable, long‑term stewardship of our natural resources; I’m wary of sudden policy shifts that could jeopardize the safety of our farms and homes. Watching my parents and now my own grandchildren age has made the security of pensions and accessible health care a personal priority; I want a system that honors the contributions of people who have spent their lives in the fields and factories. The church I attend teaches me to consider the common good, and my involvement with the local water board has taught me that practical, consensus‑driven solutions often work best for rural areas. Because the CDA’s emphasis on responsible guardianship of the land, support for families, and a balanced approach to social welfare aligns with the needs I see around me, I will cast my vote for them in the upcoming election.
